FloppyData is far cheaper: $10 for 10 GB against $35 at Decodo, and $100 for 100 GB against $275, with one balance across residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Decodo is the safer and more capable network: a clearly published 115M+ pool, ZIP and ASN targeting, near-perfect independent success rates, a free trial and scraping APIs for harder targets. For experiments and easy targets, FloppyData saves money; for business-critical scraping, Decodo is worth the premium.

FloppyData and Decodo appeal to different instincts. FloppyData is a young Dubai-registered provider charging a flat $1/GB on one balance that covers residential, mobile and datacenter traffic. Decodo, the former Smartproxy, is one of the most proven mid-market networks, with a 115M+ advertised pool, near-perfect success rates in independent benchmarks and scraping APIs. blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData is a young budget provider registered in Dubai that launched around 2024. Its pitch is radical simplicity: one balance at a flat $1/GB that you can spend on residential, mobile or datacenter rotating traffic, plus static residential and datacenter IPs sold in monthly bundles. Its residential page lists home ISP IPs in 148 countries and 442 cities. The company also offers a free cloud anti-detect browser that runs on its proxies. Its advertised 65M+ IP figure has been questioned by some reviewers, and user reviews are mixed.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
Decodo in 2026: what you get

Decodo (formerly Smartproxy) sits between the budget brands and the enterprise giants. It gives every customer the full 115M+ residential pool, city and ZIP targeting, and a self-service dashboard that most people can configure in minutes. Proxyway's annual tests ranked its pool second only to Oxylabs in size among the providers it tested, at a price well below enterprise level, which is why Decodo shows up on almost every shortlist.

Strengths: Large 115M+ pool at a mid-market price; Near-perfect success rates in independent tests; Clean, fast self-service onboarding; Scraping APIs available when raw proxies are not enough. Weak spots: Plan traffic does not roll over; Published pricing stops at 100 GB; beyond that you need a quote; More expensive per GB than budget brands.
Pricing: FloppyData vs Decodo

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.

Decodo sells residential traffic at $4/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, or on monthly plans: 3 GB for $11.25 ($3.75/GB), 10 GB for $35, 25 GB at $3.25/GB, 50 GB for $150 and 100 GB for $275 ($2.75/GB). Top-ups are billed at your plan's rate, so you are not pushed into the next tier.

At 10 GB a month, FloppyData is the cheaper option at about $10 against $35 for Decodo, roughly 71% less. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $100 with FloppyData and $275 with Decodo: a 64% saving in FloppyData's favour. Both FloppyData and Decodo work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)' and Decodo lists '115M+'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, FloppyData lists 148 (residential) countries and Decodo lists 195+. On targeting, FloppyData offers country and city, while Decodo offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions, and Decodo offers rotating or sticky sessions with configurable duration. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Decodo wins. The deciding factor for Decodo: a large pool and near-perfect benchmark success rates. The limitation on the FloppyData side: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.
SERP and rank tracking: Decodo. Decodo has the edge here. Why: a dedicated SERP scraping API plus city targeting. How FloppyData compares: workable for light tasks.

Social media and multi-account management: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. FloppyData: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser. Decodo: sticky sessions, sub-users and an easy dashboard. Let price and the countries you need decide.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Decodo. Decodo has the edge here. Why: ZIP targeting and a ready-made e-commerce API. How FloppyData compares: city targeting at a flat rate.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Decodo. Decodo has the edge here. Why: wide coverage with city and ASN targeting. How FloppyData compares: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: a flat $1/GB on any volume. The limitation on the Decodo side: it is mid-priced, not cheap.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Decodo: Free trial (about 100 MB) on residential. Verification and payment rules differ too. FloppyData: Light. Decodo: Light KYC; checks on some targets. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test FloppyData and Decodo before you commit
The quickest way to choose between FloppyData and Decodo is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations; Decodo: free trial (about 100 MB) on residential).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, FloppyData comes out ahead in 1, Decodo in 4, and 1 is a tie. That makes Decodo the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments, while Decodo is strongest for small and mid-size scraping teams. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.

Small budgets and experiments
Multi-account work using the free cloud browser
Buyers who want residential and mobile without separate plans
Decodo is the better pick for:
Small and mid-size scraping teams
Developers who want enterprise-like quality without contracts
Mixed workloads that may grow into scraping APIs
